HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Tools & Fix-It — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the fixing kit with its one rule riding alongside: tools are for fixing, real tools are used with a grown-up — and the hammer gets its honest debut.

What is this?

The fix-it team: the hammer drives nails, the screwdriver twists screws, the saw cuts (grown-ups only), and the toolbox is the home that latches them all in.

What does it mean?

Curiosity about tools is not misbehavior — it is engineering interest with nowhere to go. One real hammering session, goggles on, is worth a year of don’t-touch.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card, a small hammer, a block of scrap wood, two nails started by you, and child-size goggles if you have them. The saw and the screwdriver stay demonstrated.

Why this matters

The toolbox latch is the lesson’s quiet star: tools live in their home and come out for jobs. The click of the latch closing is the ritual ending of every fix-it session.

What it teaches

Hammer control (aim, swing, follow-through), respect for edged tools, and the fix-it identity — broken things are projects, not tragedies.

Words to learn

hammerscrewdriversawtoolboxnailsfix

Say this to your child

“"Tools and fix-it! The hammer goes bang, the screwdriver goes twist, the saw is a grown-up machine. Today YOU are the fixer — goggles on, one nail at a time."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "the fix-it team sleeps in the toolbox — let us meet them."
  2. Open the toolbox together and name everyone: hammer, screwdriver, saw — each with its one job.
  3. Hammer debut: goggles on, nails started by the grown-up, the child drives them in — real wood, real sound, real pride.
  4. Screwdriver turn: one big screw in a soft block, twist, twist, twist.
  5. The saw is only waved at: back and forth motion in the air, and the rule said kindly — saws are grown-up tools, always.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Tools and Fix-It" sit over a claw hammer with a pink grip, a red-handled screwdriver, a hand saw, and a latched two-tier toolbox.

Ask your child

"Which tool goes bang?" (the hammer) "Which tool twists?" (the screwdriver) "Where do the tools sleep?" (the toolbox — latched)

What your child can say or do

Your child might carry the goggles everywhere for a week, fix toys that were never broken, or close the toolbox latch with the gravity of a master mechanic.

Out in the real world

The fix-it instinct lasts: a child who has hammered real nails builds, repairs and helps for years. Every parent of a teenager with a flat-pack wardrobe thanks this lesson.

Try it together

Fix-It Clinic: gather one squeaky toy, one loose screw, one wobbly thing (all pre-approved) — the child diagnoses, you assist, the hammer or screwdriver does its true job, the latch clicks shut. Clinic closed.

Staying safe

Real tools, one rule, said the same way every time: tools come out for fixing, with a grown-up, and go home to the toolbox after. The saw is demonstrated in the air and never nearer. Goggles first, hammer second.

This lesson pairs with the Tools & Fix-It flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.
